task.goal: Reduce lost medication instruction sheets in a shared home while keeping them private.
hard_constraints: Two adults, existing folders and no scanning service or new lockbox.
Do not change doses or replace clinician advice; each person controls their own papers.
Test retrieval time and misfiling after one month without exposing diagnoses.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One private home for each person’s sheets
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make a single, predictable storage location the main safeguard against loss. Each adult chooses a neutral symbol for their existing folder and keeps it in a fixed shelf position. Inside, place instruction sheets in closed envelopes, with one instruction set per envelope. The owner assigns each envelope a neutral code and files it in code order. A private paper key inside the folder connects codes to the owner’s descriptions. Labels visible on the shelf contain no medication names or diagnoses.

Each adult handles only their own contents and returns an envelope immediately after reading it. New sheets go directly into that person’s folder; the owner decides how to distinguish current and older instructions without changing the instructions or discarding anything on the other person’s behalf.

This needs existing folders, envelopes, paper labels and enough shelf space. It could work because every sheet has one destination, reducing decisions about where to put it. It assumes both adults accept the return habit. Closed envelopes provide everyday visual privacy, but do not prevent deliberate access; this is unsuitable if privacy requires protection from intentional snooping.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before setup, each owner privately times retrieval of two instruction sets from their current arrangement. After one month, repeat with the same sets, starting from the same location. Each owner also checks whether their sheets are in their assigned envelopes and folder, reporting only elapsed times and a misfiling count. Keep names, contents and the private key out of shared results. No improvement in retrieval, or any increase in misfiling, challenges the benefit of the fixed-home rule.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A private locator index across existing folders
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Keep papers in the existing folders that each owner finds useful, but introduce a private address system. Each adult gives their folders neutral location codes and their instruction envelopes neutral item codes. A paper locator, kept inside that adult’s own closed envelope on the shelf, maps their personally meaningful descriptions to folder and envelope codes. Exterior labels disclose only codes. Each person alone creates and updates their locator and handles their papers.

The main mechanism is separating finding a document from remembering where it was filed. This can suit someone whose instruction sheets belong with several different groups of paperwork and who would otherwise create duplicate or competing storage places. Whenever the owner moves an instruction envelope, they update its address immediately. New sheets receive an address before filing.

Implementation requires only existing folders, envelopes, paper labels and shelf space. It assumes the owner can maintain and interpret a short index. Its main weakness is an outdated locator: it adds a maintenance step and may be slower than a single folder for a small collection. Envelopes must conceal their contents adequately; coded labels alone do not provide access control.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Record private retrieval times for two existing instruction sets before adding the locator. After one month, each owner retrieves those sets using their index and privately checks every indexed address against the actual envelope location. Share only retrieval times and counts of incorrect addresses or misfiled sheets. Compare against the original arrangement: slower retrieval or stale addresses would argue against retaining the index. Do not copy medication descriptions into the shared results.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A visible checkout signal for papers in use
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a circulation rule to address sheets that disappear after someone reads or carries them. Each adult keeps their instruction sets in closed, neutrally coded envelopes in their own existing folder. For each envelope, make a matching paper label that normally rests inside the folder beside it. When the owner removes an envelope, they leave its label protruding from the folder as a checkout signal. The label shows only the neutral code.

Each adult also designates one closed envelope on the shelf as their temporary return pocket. After use, papers go either directly back into their coded envelope or into that owner’s return pocket. At a personally chosen daily routine, the owner checks protruding labels, retrieves outstanding papers and empties their return pocket. Neither adult opens or sorts the other’s papers.

The mechanism makes unfinished returns noticeable and gives loose sheets a defined landing place. It needs envelopes, labels and existing folders, and assumes most losses occur during use rather than initial filing. It will fail if checkout signals are routinely skipped or ignored. Neutral signals conceal medical content but reveal that paperwork is outstanding; both adults must find that acceptable. Closed envelopes offer visual privacy, not security against deliberate opening.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before starting, privately time retrieval of two instruction sets and count sheets outside their intended locations. After one month, repeat and have each owner inspect their own checkout signals and return pocket. Report only times, misfiling counts and unmatched-signal counts. Compare with the original arrangement. Persistent outstanding signals, accumulated return-pocket papers or unchanged retrieval times would suggest that the circulation routine adds work without solving the loss problem.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Move the folder, keep the sheets together
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make each adult’s existing folder a portable reading surface: bring the whole folder to wherever instructions are needed, open it flat, and read sheets resting inside it. Individual sheets never travel separately around the home. After reading, the owner closes the papers inside an envelope and the folder, then returns the whole folder to the shelf.

The main mechanism is reducing separation during handling. A whole folder is more noticeable than a loose sheet, and keeping it underneath the papers makes it easier to gather everything before leaving the reading spot. This differs from tracking individual documents: it prevents a common opportunity for separation rather than recording where a removed sheet went.

Each adult chooses a neutral exterior label and controls all organization inside their own folder. Envelopes conceal instruction text when the folder is closed. Neither adult checks, sorts or returns the other’s contents. Keep the original instructions intact; this changes paper handling only, without interpreting instructions or changing doses.

Implementation needs two existing folders, sufficiently large envelopes, paper labels and shelf space. It assumes each collection is small enough to carry comfortably and most use happens at home. It may offer little benefit if losses happen before papers reach the folder, or if individual sheets must frequently accompany appointments. Closed folders and envelopes provide visual privacy, but cannot prevent deliberate opening.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before starting, each owner privately times retrieval of two instruction sheets using their current arrangement and counts missing or incorrectly filed sheets. After one month, repeat retrieval from the same starting point, including opening the envelope and finding the actual sheet. Each owner privately checks their own folder and usual reading locations for separated or misfiled sheets. Share only elapsed times and counts, with no document titles, medication names or diagnoses. Compare with the original arrangement: continued loose-sheet losses or consistently slower retrieval would challenge the approach. This small check can reveal practical failure, but cannot establish long-term reliability.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Check papers before leaving their source
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Prevent loss before instruction sheets reach home by making collection and transport a deliberate checkpoint. Each adult takes an empty, opaque envelope to appointments or other places where they expect paper instructions. Before leaving, the owner gathers any sheets actually issued, checks that all pages of each instruction set are present, and puts them directly into the envelope. If a referenced page appears absent, they ask the issuing staff about it; they do not reconstruct medical instructions themselves.

At home, the owner transfers the papers into their existing folder and checks the page count against a small tally written inside the transport envelope. The envelope stays with the papers until that check is complete. Exterior labels contain only a neutral personal symbol. Each adult handles and checks only their own papers; the other adult does not act as an auditor.

The mechanism is checking completeness at the point where missing papers can still be recovered, then preserving the collected batch during transport. This targets losses before filing, which a home storage rule cannot repair. It requires envelopes, paper labels, existing folders and shelf space. It assumes at least some losses occur during collection or travel and that the owner can pause to check the papers. It provides visual privacy, not protection against deliberate opening. Existing instructions remain intact, and clinical advice and doses are unchanged.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before starting, each adult privately times retrieval of two existing instruction sets and counts missing or misfiled sheets. After one month, repeat those retrievals and inspect their own filing. Also check whether any newly received batches arrived with fewer pages than recorded at collection. Share only retrieval times, misfiling counts and batch discrepancies, without titles or medical information. Compare with the previous handling routine. Continued transport discrepancies or increased misfiling challenge the approach. If no new sheets arrive during the month, the main mechanism remains untested; the retrieval check alone cannot establish its benefit.

EXPAND.title: Read sheets in place to prevent circulation losses
EXPAND.proposal:
Each adult keeps their instruction sheets in their own existing folder inside an opaque envelope on the shelf. The owner consults papers at that shelf and returns them before moving away. The mechanism removes most transport and return steps: finding instructions need not require carrying them elsewhere. This targets losses during use, whereas the earlier fixed-home proposal still depends on remembering to return papers after use.

Each owner places incoming sheets in their folder and chooses a usable internal order. Only that owner opens or arranges the contents. Exterior labels use neutral symbols. If someone needs the instructions beside them for safe use, needs better lighting, or must take them to an appointment, they take the whole closed folder; storage convenience must not interfere with following clinician advice. Afterward, the owner returns it to the shelf. Neither person retrieves or interprets instructions for the other.

This requires existing folders, concealing envelopes, labels, and a shelf where the owner can comfortably consult papers without another person overlooking them. It assumes many consultations can happen there. Envelopes provide visual privacy, not protection against deliberate opening. If the shelf cannot support private, comfortable reading, this route is unsuitable.
EXPAND.experiment: Each adult independently owns a one-month trial. Before starting, privately time retrieval of two instruction sets using a simple fixed-home arrangement. After one month, repeat and count misfiled or missing sheets privately. Also record consultation inconvenience and occasions when taking papers elsewhere was necessary. Share only times and counts. Stop the in-place rule immediately if it makes following instructions harder or exposes contents. Retain it only if retrieval or misfiling improves enough to justify the inconvenience compared with ordinary take-and-return storage; otherwise restore the simpler arrangement.

EXPAND.title: File by arrival order without assigning categories
EXPAND.proposal:
Each adult uses one existing folder containing a closed, opaque envelope. New instruction sheets go at the front in arrival order, with pages received together kept together. The owner writes only the receipt date on a folded paper label around each group. To retrieve instructions, the owner searches from newest to oldest, opening groups privately. No item codes, category decisions, or locator updates are required.

The mechanism removes classification work at entry. The earlier fixed-home route requires choosing an envelope and maintaining a code or key; papers can remain loose while those decisions are deferred. Here, entry is a single insertion, even when the owner does not yet know how a document should be classified. Dates indicate arrival only, never which instructions are clinically current.

Each person alone inserts, searches, and returns their groups. After consultation, the owner restores the group to its date position. If a group is found loose, its owner restores it using the receipt label; if its date is unknown, the owner places it at the back with an undated label. Nobody discards or resolves conflicting instructions for the other adult; clinical uncertainty goes to the appropriate clinician or pharmacist.

This needs folders, envelopes, and labels. It suits modest collections where recent papers are commonly needed. Older-document searches may be slow, and closed envelopes do not prevent intentional access.
EXPAND.experiment: Each owner runs a one-month trial against their own baseline using a fixed folder with coded envelopes. Privately time retrieval of one recent and one older instruction set before setup and after one month; count misfiled groups and loose sheets at both points. Track filing effort with a simple tally of entries needing extra sorting. Share only times and counts. Stop if page grouping becomes unreliable or an older set cannot be located. Reject this route if easier entry is outweighed by slower retrieval or more misfiling.

EXPAND.title: Use an owner-to-owner custody rule during household tidying
EXPAND.proposal:
Agree that medication papers never enter shared sorting piles, recycling, or general household folders. Each adult controls their own papers and puts them in their own closed envelope inside an existing folder on the shelf. The distinctive mechanism is a household custody boundary: it prevents another person's well-intended cleanup from breaking the connection between owner and document. This addresses a loss cause that a fixed storage location alone does not prevent.

Each owner places a neutral personal symbol on their folder and on the outside of their instruction packets. If the other adult encounters a marked, closed packet while tidying, they leave it closed and hand it directly to its owner. If the owner is unavailable, they leave it where found and mention its location without medical details. They do not open, sort, or relocate it. For an unmarked loose sheet, they avoid inspecting it to identify its owner and ask both adults to check the location privately. The owner then retrieves and files it. New papers receive the owner's neutral mark when the owner first handles them.

This needs only existing folders, envelopes, labels, and both adults' agreement. It is most promising when shared cleanup contributes to losses; it adds little if owners primarily lose papers themselves. Loose sheets may already expose content, so owners should enclose them promptly. The agreement provides everyday privacy rather than security against intentional access.
EXPAND.experiment: Each adult owns their part of a one-month trial. Record private retrieval times for two sets and misfiling counts before starting and after one month. Compare with the same fixed-home arrangement before adding the custody rule. Tally interrupted cleanups, unresolved loose-paper incidents, and accidental viewing without recording contents. Share only times and counts. Stop if leaving papers in place creates unacceptable exposure or persistent clutter. Keep the rule only if reduced loss or misfiling justifies the coordination burden; no improvement would undermine its value.

EXPAND.title: A fixed private folder with an interruption-safe intake envelope
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of “One private home for each person’s sheets.” Keep its main mechanism: each adult has one existing folder in a fixed shelf position, neutrally coded closed envelopes for individual instruction sets, and a private code key inside. Each person alone controls their papers and distinguishes current from older material without altering instructions.

Change the intake procedure to handle interrupted filing. Add one opaque envelope marked with a neutral symbol for papers awaiting assignment. If the owner cannot finish coding a new set immediately, they put the complete set there before setting it down. At their next instruction retrieval, they check this envelope first. They finish filing when practical; until then, this remains an explicitly searchable location. Nobody else clears it. If it becomes difficult to search or cannot close, the owner stops adding codes and temporarily uses the folder as one collection of enclosed, separately grouped sets until they can restore the index privately.

This uses existing folders, envelopes, paper labels and shelf space. Compared with the source, it adds one possible search location but removes the need to complete classification before papers have a protected destination. Its value depends on interrupted intake being a real cause of loss. Opaque envelopes provide visual privacy, not protection against intentional opening. Doses and clinician advice remain unchanged.
EXPAND.experiment: Each owner privately times retrieval of two chosen sets and counts misfiled or loose sets before setup. During a one-month trial, use the intake envelope whenever filing is interrupted; record only the number of such uses. After one month, repeat retrieval of the same sets, including the intake envelope in the search, and audit both locations privately. Share only elapsed times, missing or misfiled counts, and the number still awaiting assignment. Stop the added intake procedure if it creates an unsearchable backlog or makes finding needed instructions harder; return to the source’s direct-filing procedure. Retain the upgrade only if reduced loose or misplaced papers justifies its extra search step. No benefit is established in advance.

EXPAND.title: Keep each instruction packet with the item it explains
EXPAND.proposal:
Use physical association as the retrieval mechanism: for an adult whose medication already has a suitable storage place on the available shelf, keep its instruction packet immediately with its existing container, inside that adult’s closed folder. Looking for the item then brings its instructions into view without consulting a separate locator. Do not relocate medication merely to make this system work.

Each owner checks privately whether their existing folder can accommodate the relevant containers and closed instruction envelopes without crowding, obscuring essential container labels, or interfering with appropriate storage. If so, they pair each container with a neutrally marked opaque envelope. At the already occurring moment of putting a newly received item away, the owner encloses its papers and places the pair together. To consult instructions, they take the pair and return it together. Instructions covering several items stay together beside those items; the owner does not split a shared instruction set or infer which advice supersedes another. Questions about conflicting advice go to the clinician or pharmacist.

This requires suitable existing containers, sufficient folder and shelf space, envelopes and paper labels. If those prerequisites fail, use a separate private folder in a fixed shelf position instead. Compared with separate paper storage, pairing may reduce forgotten filing and searching, but makes the folder bulkier and can expose an association if left open. Each adult handles only their own contents. Closed folders and opaque envelopes must conceal contents adequately; they do not prevent deliberate access. No doses or clinical instructions change.
EXPAND.experiment: Before setup, each participating owner privately times retrieval of two instruction sets from their existing arrangement and counts misplaced sets. First inspect one proposed pairing for fit, privacy and unobstructed access to the medication; abandon pairing if any prerequisite fails. If it passes, trial it for one month. Then repeat the same retrieval tasks and privately check every pair for missing, mismatched or loose instructions. Share only times and counts, without container names, envelope codes or diagnoses. Stop immediately if pairing interferes with appropriate storage, following instructions or privacy, and return papers to the owner’s fixed private folder. Keep the method only if retrieval or misfiling improves enough to justify the bulk and handling burden; its benefit remains uncertain until tested.
